content: In industrialized countries, the financial burden of addressing health issues related to free sugar intake would surpass the total healthcare resources allocated for children in most lower-income countries. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed guidelines on sugar intake for adults and children following evidence-based procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. This process was led by the WHO Department of Nutrition for Health and Development (NHD) in collaboration with the WHO Secretariat and guided by the WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guideline Development. The committee included representatives from all WHO departments with an interest in providing scientific advice on nutrition. Two additional groups were formed to support the guideline development: the Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG) Subgroup on Diet and Health and an external peer-review group. The NUGAG subgroup consisted of experts with prior experience in WHO consultations or advisory panels, as well as others identified through open calls for experts. Representatives of commercial organizations were excluded to avoid conflicts of interest. External resource persons, including subject-matter experts and systematic review methodologists, were invited to provide technical input but did not participate in decision-making. The external peer-review group included representatives from public institutions, subject-matter experts (including those in dentistry), and other stakeholders such as practitioners and journal editors. This group reviewed the draft guidelines to identify errors or missing information before finalization. Public consultations were also held during the planning stages, inviting comments on the scope of the guidelines and specific research questions. Feedback from these consultations was reviewed and incorporated into the guideline development process. The guideline's scope and evidence appraisal were based on questions addressing the needs of WHO Member States and international partners. These questions were structured using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) format. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were commissioned to address these questions, focusing on the effects of free sugar intake on weight gain and dental caries—two critical health outcomes. While other outcomes, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease, were considered, the focus remained on weight gain and dental caries due to their direct association with free sugar intake. The systematic review on body weight examined whether changes in free sugar intake influenced body weight in adults and children. The evidence quality was considered moderate for adults and children regarding reduced sugar intake and body weight reduction. However, the evidence linking increased sugar intake to weight gain in children was of low quality. The review on dental caries assessed the relationship between free sugar intake and dental caries in adults and children. Positive associations were observed across all age groups, geographic regions, and decades of publication. The evidence suggested that higher free sugar intake was associated with increased dental caries, even in populations exposed to fluoride. The WHO recommends reducing free sugar intake throughout the life course. Specifically, it strongly recommends limiting free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake and conditionally suggests further reducing it to below 5% of total energy intake. Free sugars include monosaccharides and disaccharides added to foods and beverages, as well as sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, fruit juices, and fruit juice concentrates. These recommendations are based on evidence linking free sugar intake to body weight and dental caries. Reducing free sugar intake is not associated with harm and is considered beneficial for minimizing lifelong risks of dental caries and other health complications. The guidelines will be disseminated through the WHO e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA), the NHD website, and mailing lists. Policymakers and program managers are encouraged to assess current free sugar intake levels in their populations and implement public health interventions to reduce intake where necessary.
